content.p: Salvatore Riina, the Sicilian Mafia boss known to newspapers as the "boss of bosses", died in a prison hospital in Parma on 17 November 2017, the day after his 87th birthday. He had been serving 26 life sentences for murders committed between 1969 and 1992. He had spent the last years of his life under the strict isolation regime Italy reserved for senior mafiosi, and his death ended the career of a man who had taken control of Cosa Nostra in the 1970s and then waged a campaign of killings against rivals, police officers and anti-Mafia judges.
content.h2: From Corleone to the top of Cosa Nostra
content.p: Riina was born on 16 November 1930 in Corleone, a hill town inland from Palermo whose name Mario Puzo borrowed for the Godfather novels. He grew up poor. Al Jazeera dates his first conviction for murder to 1949, when he was 19. The Local reported that he later served six years for manslaughter after a killing in an argument, and that he came out to become a foot soldier for Luciano Leggio, a volatile boss.

In 1969 Riina went into hiding. The Associated Press reported that the state had ordered him to leave Sicily after he finished a five-year sentence for Mafia association. Daily Trust reported that he remained on the island for the next 24 years while the authorities searched for him.

Riina's rise came through a series of killings. Daily Trust reported that he helped Leggio kill the Corleone boss, and that he later led a hit squad, alongside his childhood friend Bernardo Provenzano, that targeted the Palermo boss Michele Cavataio. Leggio was arrested in 1974, and Daily Trust says Riina became boss then. The Local dates his takeover to the end of the 1970s. The sources differ on the date, but agree that the Corleonesi clan came to dominate Cosa Nostra in that decade.

The Associated Press and the Mining Journal, which carried its report, described Palermo in those years as a city where murders happened almost every day. Rival bosses were shot in the 1970s and early 1980s while Riina built his position. He broke many of the organisation's own rules, including the custom of sparing women and children from gunfire. The Local reported that he took charge of the organisation's main businesses, from drug trafficking to kidnapping and racketeering.

The sources describe a leader who avoided public view. The Associated Press said that for years the only photograph the authorities had of him dated from more than three decades earlier. Former members who had defected said he came and went as he pleased while he was Italy's most wanted man.

Riina stayed in Sicily for almost a quarter of a century. Time magazine, writing in June 1996, said the Mafia had been pressed by "a few gutsy judges" and a growing number of police officers, but still reached into business and politics. It described Cosa Nostra as about 180 families with some 5,000 members at that point.

The Associated Press quoted a former Palermo anti-Mafia magistrate, Alfonso Sabella, who said that up to the moment of Riina's death he was still the "capo" of Cosa Nostra. That is the view of an investigator, not a court finding.

The most notorious murders attributed to Riina were the bombings that killed two of Italy's leading anti-Mafia magistrates. Giovanni Falcone was killed in 1992, and Paolo Borsellino about two months later. The Local reported that the judges had worked to put more than 300 mobsters on trial in 1987. The Associated Press said prosecutors accused Riina of masterminding a campaign to kill prosecutors, police officers and others pursuing Cosa Nostra, and that the state responded with a much harder line against the mob after the two deaths.

Al Jazeera reported that Riina had said the prosecutors would be "slaughtered like tuna" before the killings. The Local reported that he also ordered the kidnapping of a 13-year-old boy, who was held to stop the boy's father from talking, and that the boy was killed.

The Local reported that after Riina's arrest, the organisation carried out bombings in Rome, Milan and Florence that killed ten people, in revenge for his capture and for a new law that kept jailed mobsters in isolation.

Riina was arrested in Palermo on 15 January 1993. The Associated Press reported that investigators working with turncoats located him and blocked his car on a city road. According to the Il Fatto Quotidiano article written in 2023 by the chief prosecutor who took office in Palermo that day, the arrest was carried out by Carabinieri officers from the ROS unit in Palermo, led by the officer Sergio De Caprio, known as "Ultimo". The article credits a former Riina driver, Baldassare Di Maggio, who had been arrested in northern Italy a few days earlier and who agreed to give information.

The arrest was then followed by a dispute that is still discussed. Riina had been stopped outside an area where his home was, and the house had not been identified precisely. The Il Fatto article says the prosecutors wanted an immediate search, but the Carabinieri asked for more time. Surveillance of the house was suspended, the article says, without informing the prosecutors. When the villa was entered, it was found empty of documents and notes. The article quotes a 2021 memoir by Mario Mori, the Ros commander, in which Mori wrote that the decision not to search at once, proposed by De Caprio and supported by Mori, prevailed.

The Local's 2015 report says the house was on Via Bernini, which had been the hideout where Riina lived until his arrest. In 2015 the building was opened as a Carabinieri police station, with Interior Minister Angelino Alfano attending. "The state won, and the Mafia has lost," Alfano said at the ceremony, according to The Local.

The Associated Press said his first life sentence came in 1987, imposed while he was a fugitive, on murder and drug-trafficking charges. He was serving 26 life terms at his death. The Associated Press reported that he steadfastly refused to collaborate with investigators after his arrest, and that RAI, the Italian state radio, described his silence as "mute as a tomb".

He was held under a special regime designed to isolate senior mafiosi, with limited contact and time outside his cell. The Local reported that in 2009 he broke the Mafia's code of silence by admitting his membership of Cosa Nostra. In 2017, The Local said, he was caught on a wiretap saying he "regrets nothing", and in July 2017 he asked to be released on the grounds of serious illness. The request was refused.

Italian prosecutor Franco Roberti, who retired as national anti-Mafia prosecutor that month, told the Associated Press that Riina had never repented. "He was still considered the 'boss of bosses,' even in prison," Roberti said.

Riina was placed in a medically induced coma after two operations in the weeks before his death. The Italian Justice Ministry allowed his family to visit him at the hospital on 16 November, his birthday. He died in the prisoners' wing of the Parma hospital in the early hours of 17 November, at about 3:37 a.m., according to Il Globo. AFP, as published by The Local, said it was just before 4:00 a.m.

The reports disagree about the cause. The Local, citing AFP, said the Italian government had described his death as following a battle with cancer. Daily Trust reported kidney cancer, a heart condition and Parkinson's disease. The Justice Ministry confirmed the death without giving details, the Associated Press reported.

The Italian bishops' conference ruled out a public church funeral. Michele Pennisi, archbishop of Monreale, whose diocese includes Corleone, said Riina's death "ends the delusion of the Cosa Nostra boss of bosses' omnipotence", but warned that "the Mafia has not been defeated". He said a public funeral would not be allowed because Riina was a "public sinner", and that a private prayer at the cemetery would be considered if the family asked.

Roberti, the prosecutor, said Cosa Nostra would likely face a power struggle at the top after the death. He also said the organisation had been less visible in recent years than the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta, which The Associated Press described as having spread north through Italy on the proceeds of cocaine trafficking.

Riina's sons were also involved in the Mafia. Al Jazeera said that his son Giovanni, arrested in 1997, received a life term in 2001 for four killings, and that another son, Giuseppe, was convicted in 2004 of extortion and money laundering.
